entries.exactPassage: Dollar-Cost Averaging = Consistency + Time → Mathematically Superior
entries.concern: The unqualified mathematical-superiority claim has no comparator or conditions. Regular contributions do not universally beat investing a lump sum already available, and do not guarantee growth.
entries.proposedWording: Dollar-cost averaging = regular contributions + time. It can reduce timing decisions and buy more units when prices are lower; outcomes depend on prices, costs, resources and the comparison being made.

relatedPassages.exactPassage: Remove Your Emotions. Automate Your Investing. Let Math Do the Work.

entries.exactPassage: Here’s the tension: dollar-cost averaging works because it removes emotion. But removing emotion feels wrong. When the market drops 20% and everyone is panicking, your brain screams at you to stop investing — to wait, to protect, to hide. Continuing to invest in that moment feels reckless. It is the opposite of reckless. It is the moment when your money buys the most. The people who keep investing through crashes are the ones who build wealth. The people who stop are the ones who lock in their losses. The strategy requires doing what feels wrong. And that — doing what feels wrong because the math says it is right — is the hardest discipline in investing.
entries.category: Material distinction and specific affordability concern
entries.concern: Pausing new contributions is not equivalent to selling holdings and realising a loss. The passage encourages continuing through any crash without changed needs/affordability, and implies wealth follows for everyone who continues.
entries.proposedWording: Market falls can make sticking to a considered plan difficult. Review your goals, holdings, access needs and affordability before changing it. Pausing contributions and selling investments are different decisions; neither consistency nor a falling price guarantees future growth.

entries.exactPassage: Failure signal: If I skip more than 3 months of contributions in any year, I must set up an automatic debit order.
entries.category: Specific affordability concern and missing risk context
entries.concern: The mandatory automatic debit response can commit an unaffordable payment when income or essential needs change. A long horizon can change risk capacity but does not guarantee smooth returns.
entries.proposedWording: If contributions are missed, review income, essential needs and the plan. An affordable automatic payment may help if appropriate; adjusting the amount or timeline may be necessary. A long horizon does not remove market risk.

entries.exactPassage: Thabo pauses. He had not built a buffer. He adds one: in months where income drops below R1,500, the investment drops to R100. The R200 difference goes to emergency savings. The plan survives because it flexes.
entries.concern: The reallocation is100+200=300, the same original outflow. A more liquid destination can improve resilience but does not itself create surplus in a low-income month or prove the plan survives.
entries.proposedWording: Thabo first checks income, essential costs and existing reserves for a bad month. He distinguishes reducing total contributions to what is affordable from moving money between investing and accessible emergency savings; the revised total and destination must both fit his circumstances.
